title: Admiral Car Insurance Review
meta_title: Admiral Car Insurance Review 2026: MultiCar and Cover
meta_description: Admiral's comprehensive cover is 5-star Defaqto rated. What MultiCar saves, what each tier includes, and the two things to check before you buy.
intro:
Admiral's comprehensive car insurance carries a 5-star Defaqto rating, the top mark an independent assessor gives, and the range runs from Platinum down through Gold and Admiral. Windscreen cover, a courtesy car at approved garages and child car seat cover come as standard on the comprehensive tiers, and Platinum folds in European cover and roadside breakdown so there is nothing left to bolt on.

MultiCar is the reason most households end up here. Insure two or three vehicles on a single policy, each keeping its own no-claims bonus, and the combined price is usually below the sum of separate policies. It bites hardest for parents insuring a young driver alongside their own cars, where premiums in isolation are punishing. There is a MultiCover equivalent for bundling car and home.

The excess options are unusually granular too — £50 steps from £0 to £500, then £700, £750 and £1,000 — which gives real control over the premium. Two things to read before buying: the cut-price Essential tier is a different product from the rest of the range, and the admin fees are worth pricing in. Both are covered below.

sections.heading: MultiCar: the actual reason to choose Admiral
sections.html:
MultiCar lets a household insure several vehicles under one policy, each with its own no-claims bonus, at a combined price usually below the sum of separate policies.

It suits a specific household shape: two working adults with a car each, or parents insuring a young driver alongside their own vehicles. The second case is where it bites hardest, because young-driver premiums are punishing in isolation and the MultiCar structure softens that considerably.

MultiCover extends the same idea to home insurance, bundling car and home for a further discount.

One thing to check rather than assume: the vehicles generally need to be at the same address. Adding a car kept at a student address or a second home is where MultiCar quotes tend to fall over, and it is worth confirming before you build a renewal plan around it.

If you are a single-car household with no home insurance to bundle, the main argument for Admiral disappears and you should be comparing purely on price and cover level.

sections.heading: Where the cover is genuinely good
sections.html:
Set Essential aside and the rest of the range is strong.

Platinum bundles European cover, windscreen, courtesy car and roadside breakdown into one policy, which removes the add-on juggling that makes comparison sites so misleading. Gold is the same shape with breakdown optional.

The voluntary excess range is unusually granular — £50 increments from £0 to £500, then £700, £750 and £1,000. Most insurers offer four or five options. That granularity lets you tune the premium precisely rather than jumping between wide bands.

Child car seat cover as standard across all comprehensive tiers is a small but genuine inclusion; seats must be replaced after any impact and they are not cheap.

Courtesy cars come through Admiral-approved garages, which is standard practice but does mean you use their repair network rather than your own choice of garage.

sections.heading: Essential is not a cheaper version of the same policy
sections.html:
It is a materially different product, and the two omissions matter.

No windscreen cover. A replacement windscreen on a modern car with camera-based driver assistance frequently runs past £500 once recalibration is included. On every other Admiral comprehensive tier that is covered. On Essential you pay it.

No European cover. Drive to France on an Essential policy and you are running on the legal minimum required in that country, not comprehensive cover. Damage to your own vehicle is not covered.

The Defaqto exclusion is the clearest signal available. Admiral's comprehensive range is 5-star rated and Essential specifically is not included in that rating — an independent assessor declining to put it in the same category as its siblings.

Essential makes sense for an older, low-value car that never leaves the UK, where you have decided a cracked windscreen is a cost you would absorb anyway. For anything else the saving is smaller than the exposure.

sections.heading: The admin fees deserve attention
sections.html:
Around £15 to amend a policy, and £60 to £160 to cancel, depending on circumstances.

The cancellation range is the one to note. If you sell a car mid-term, write it off, or simply find a better price at month seven, you are paying a fee that can approach the cost of two months' premium. That materially changes the maths on switching mid-policy.

Amendment fees add up too if your circumstances move — a change of address, a change of job title, adding a named driver. None are large individually, but a policy that gets amended three times has quietly cost £45 more than the quoted premium.

Compare that against insurers offering free amendments if you expect your details to change during the year.

verdict: Strong if you have more than one vehicle, or a car and home policy to bundle — MultiCar and MultiCover are genuinely competitive and hard to beat by shopping separately. Take Platinum or Gold rather than Essential: the missing windscreen and European cover are worth more than the saving, and Defaqto's refusal to include Essential in the 5-star rating tells you what an independent assessor makes of it. If you are a single-car household with no bundle to build, compare on price like any other insurer, and factor the £60–£160 cancellation fee into any plan to switch mid-term.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Admiral and Admiral Essential?
faqs.a: Essential removes windscreen cover and European cover, and is excluded from Admiral's 5-star Defaqto rating. The standard Admiral, Gold and Platinum tiers include windscreen cover and carry the rating.

faqs.q: How does MultiCar work?
faqs.a: You insure several vehicles under one policy, each keeping its own no-claims bonus, at a combined price usually lower than separate policies. Vehicles generally need to be at the same address — confirm this before relying on it.

faqs.q: What are Admiral's admin fees?
faqs.a: Roughly £15 to amend a policy and £60 to £160 to cancel, depending on circumstances. The cancellation fee is worth factoring in if you might switch mid-term or sell the car.

faqs.q: Is a courtesy car included?
faqs.a: Yes with comprehensive cover, provided the repair goes through an Admiral-approved garage. Using your own choice of garage may forfeit it.

faqs.q: Does Admiral cover driving in Europe?
faqs.a: Platinum includes European cover. Essential excludes it entirely, leaving you on the legal minimum abroad rather than comprehensive cover.

title: Admiral Home Insurance Review: Buildings and Contents Cover
meta_title: Admiral Buildings and Contents Insurance Review 2026
meta_description: Admiral home and contents insurance compared across all three tiers. Contents limits, the £2,000 single-item rule, and what MultiCover saves.
intro:
Admiral sells buildings and contents insurance across three tiers — Admiral, Gold and Platinum — and the differences between them are more specific than the names suggest.

Buildings cover is unlimited rebuild cost on all three, which removes the single biggest risk in home insurance: under-insuring the structure. Where they diverge is contents, which runs £100,000 on Admiral, £125,000 on Gold and £150,000 on Platinum, and in what comes included rather than as a paid extra.

The clause that catches most people is the same at every tier: any single item worth more than £2,000 must be specified individually or it is not covered for its full value. That applies to an engagement ring, a road bike, a laptop, a watch. It is the most common reason a contents claim pays out less than the owner expected.

sections.heading: Which tier, decided by what is included rather than the headline
sections.html:
The contents limits — £100,000, £125,000, £150,000 — are a distraction for most households. Very few people have £100,000 of contents, so that ceiling rarely binds.

What actually separates the tiers is what stops being an add-on:

  • Admiral — accidental damage, home emergency and legal cover are all optional extras.
  • Gold — audiovisual accidental damage and home emergency (£500) are included. Full contents accidental damage and legal remain optional.
  • Platinum — everything is included: full accidental damage, home emergency at £1,000, and legal cover up to £100,000.

Price the add-ons individually before assuming the base tier is cheaper. Buying Admiral plus accidental damage plus home emergency plus legal frequently costs more than Platinum with all four built in, and leaves you with a lower home emergency limit.

Accidental damage is the add-on worth having if you have children, pets or hard flooring. It covers the spilled paint, the foot through the ceiling, the television knocked off its stand — none of which are covered by standard contents cover.

sections.heading: Unlimited rebuild cost removes the classic mistake
sections.html:
Under-insurance on buildings is the most expensive error in home insurance, and it is easy to make. Rebuild cost is not market value — it is what it would cost to demolish and reconstruct the property, and on older or unusual houses it can exceed what the house would sell for.

Get that figure too low and insurers apply average: insure for half the true rebuild cost and a £20,000 claim pays £10,000, even though £20,000 is well within your sum insured.

Admiral offers unlimited rebuild cost cover on all three tiers, which sidesteps the problem entirely. You are not asked to estimate a figure you have no way of calculating accurately.

For a period property, a thatched roof, a converted barn or anything non-standard, that is worth more than a small premium difference elsewhere.

sections.heading: The £2,000 rule is the one to act on
sections.html:
Contents cover pays out per item as well as in total. Admiral's unspecified single-item limit is £2,000 across all tiers. Anything worth more must be listed by name on the policy.

What that catches in an ordinary house:

  • An engagement or wedding ring — frequently over £2,000 on its own
  • A road or e-bike — £3,000 is unremarkable now
  • A camera body plus lenses, if claimed as one item
  • A watch, a laptop, a musical instrument

Claim for a stolen £4,500 ring that was never specified and you receive £2,000. The shortfall is not a technicality — it is what the policy says.

Do this before you buy, not at renewal: walk through the house and list anything worth more than £2,000, then declare each one. It usually adds little to the premium and it is the difference between being insured and being partly insured.

sections.heading: MultiCover, and the fees to price in
sections.html:
MultiCover discounts home insurance when you also hold Admiral car cover. If your car is already with Admiral, get the home quote before shopping elsewhere — the bundled price is often below what a standalone home policy costs.

The reverse holds too: if you are buying home insurance here and your car renews soon, price the pair together rather than separately.

Two fees to factor in. Around £15 to amend a policy, and £60 to £160 to cancel. Home policies get amended more than people expect — adding a specified item, a change after building work, a new occupant — and those £15s accumulate. The cancellation fee matters if you move house mid-term, which is common enough to price in rather than ignore.

Platinum bundles full accidental damage, £1,000 home emergency and legal cover as standard

Gold includes audiovisual accidental damage and home emergency as standard

Base Admiral tier makes accidental damage, home emergency and legal all paid extras

£60–£160 cancellation fee stings if you move house mid-term
£15 amendment fee adds up when specifying items or changing details
Contents ceilings are largely irrelevant to most households, which makes tier comparison harder than it looks
verdict: Strong on the thing that matters most — unlimited rebuild cost on buildings at every tier means you cannot under-insure the structure, which is the costliest mistake in home insurance. Compare Platinum against the base tier with add-ons bolted on before deciding; Platinum frequently wins on price and always wins on the home emergency limit. Whichever tier you take, list every item worth over £2,000 before the policy starts. If your car is already with Admiral, get the MultiCover quote first.

faqs.q: Does Admiral cover buildings and contents together?
faqs.a: Yes. You can buy buildings and contents as a combined policy across all three tiers. Buildings cover is unlimited rebuild cost; contents is capped at £100,000, £125,000 or £150,000 depending on tier.

faqs.q: What is the single-item limit?
faqs.a: £2,000. Anything worth more must be specified individually on the policy or it will only be covered up to £2,000. This catches engagement rings, bikes, watches and cameras most often.

faqs.q: Is accidental damage included?
faqs.a: Only on Platinum for full contents. Gold includes accidental damage for audiovisual equipment. On the base Admiral tier it is an optional extra for both.

faqs.q: What does unlimited rebuild cost mean?
faqs.a: You are not asked to estimate what it would cost to rebuild your home, so you cannot under-insure it. Under-insuring buildings triggers 'average', where claims are scaled down in proportion to the shortfall.

faqs.q: How much is home emergency cover?
faqs.a: £500 on the Admiral tier as an optional extra, £500 included on Gold, and £1,000 included on Platinum.

title: Admiral Motorbike Insurance Review
meta_title: Admiral Motorbike Insurance Review 2026: Multi-Bike and Cover
meta_description: Admiral motorbike insurance reviewed: multi-bike discounts, helmet and leathers cover, European use, and what the tiers actually include.
intro:
Motorbike insurance is priced on a different logic to car insurance, and the gap between a good policy and a cheap one shows up in three places: what happens to your gear, whether you can ride in Europe, and how many bikes you can put on one policy.

Admiral covers scooters, commuters, cruisers and sports bikes, with multi-bike discounts for riders who own more than one. Cover runs from third party through to comprehensive, with optional breakdown, helmet and leathers protection, and legal expenses.

The thing most riders get wrong is assuming their kit is covered. A helmet, jacket, boots and gloves easily represent £1,200 of equipment, and standard comprehensive cover does not automatically replace them after a crash.

sections.heading: Multi-bike: the main reason to be here
sections.html:
Riders who own more than one machine — a commuter and a weekend bike, a project in the garage, a classic — usually pay considerably more insuring them separately than together.

Admiral's multi-bike arrangement puts several machines on one policy with a combined discount and a single renewal date. If you own two or more bikes, this is the first quote to get.

It also works alongside MultiCar, so a bike can sit on the same household policy as cars — useful for a rider whose partner drives, or a household with a van and a bike.

Two things to confirm rather than assume: that the machines are kept at the same address, and how a claim on one affects the no-claims bonus on the others. Policies vary on the second point and it matters more than the discount.

sections.heading: Storage and security: declare it accurately
sections.html:
Motorcycle theft is concentrated and opportunistic, and insurers price it hard. Where the bike is kept overnight — locked garage, driveway, on the street — moves the premium substantially, and so do declared security measures like a ground anchor, chain, disc lock, tracker or alarm.

Declaring a garage you do not use, or security you have not fitted, is the fastest way to have a theft claim declined. Insurers investigate theft claims closely because the fraud rate is high, and the security question is the first thing they check.

Conversely, if you have fitted a Thatcham-approved immobiliser or tracker and not told them, you are paying more than you need to. Re-declare after any security upgrade.

sections.heading: Your gear is not covered by default
sections.html:
Add it up honestly. A decent helmet is £300 to £600. A textile or leather jacket, £200 to £500. Boots, gloves, trousers — another £300. Most riders are wearing £1,000 to £1,500 of equipment before the bike is considered.

Standard comprehensive cover insures the motorcycle. Riding gear is normally a separate add-on, and when you buy it there are two things to check:

  • The limit. Some policies cap gear cover at £500, which does not replace a helmet and a jacket together.
  • Whether the helmet is covered after any impact. A helmet that has been dropped or crashed in must be replaced whether or not it looks damaged — the protective structure is single-use. A policy that only pays for visible damage misses the point.

This add-on is usually cheap relative to what it covers, and it is the one most worth taking.

sections.heading: European riding and the tour trap
sections.html:
If you ride abroad, check the European allowance rather than assuming comprehensive cover follows you.

Many policies include a limited number of days of European use, and drop to third-party-only beyond it. A rider on a two-week Alpine tour can find that days eleven to fourteen are uninsured for damage to their own bike — the point at which the roads get most interesting.

Where the allowance is short, extending it for the trip is usually inexpensive. The mistake is discovering the limit after the trip rather than before.

Breakdown cover deserves the same treatment. Recovery of a motorcycle from mainland Europe is expensive and specialist, and standard UK breakdown cover generally does not extend to it.

Multi-bike generally requires machines at the same address

verdict: The strongest case for Admiral is multi-bike — if you own two or more machines, or a bike alongside household cars, the combined price is hard to beat by shopping separately. Whichever insurer you end up with, take the helmet and leathers add-on and check its limit against what you actually wear, because £1,200 of gear is not covered by a standard comprehensive policy. If you tour, confirm the European day allowance before booking rather than after, and be scrupulously accurate about where the bike is kept overnight.

faqs.q: Is my helmet and riding gear covered?
faqs.a: Not as standard. Helmet and leathers cover is normally an optional add-on. Check the limit — some cap at £500, which will not replace a helmet and jacket together — and confirm the helmet is replaced after any impact rather than only when visibly damaged.

faqs.q: Can I insure more than one bike?
faqs.a: Yes. Admiral's multi-bike arrangement covers several machines on one policy with a combined discount and one renewal date. Bikes generally need to be at the same address. Ask how a claim on one affects the no-claims bonus on the others.

faqs.q: Am I covered riding in Europe?
faqs.a: European cover is available but usually limited to a set number of days. Beyond the allowance you may drop to third-party-only. Check the limit before a long tour and extend it if needed.

faqs.q: How does where I keep the bike affect the price?
faqs.a: Substantially. A locked garage prices very differently to street parking, and declared security like a ground anchor, chain, tracker or alarm reduces the premium. Declare it accurately — theft claims are investigated closely and this is the first thing checked.

faqs.q: What does it cost to cancel?
faqs.a: Between £60 and £160 depending on circumstances, plus around £15 for amendments. Worth factoring in if you might sell the bike at the end of the season.

title: Admiral Van Insurance Review
meta_title: Admiral Van Insurance Review 2026: Cover, Tools and MultiCar
meta_description: Admiral van insurance and where it fits. Social versus commercial use, tools cover, MultiCar with your car, and the fees to know about.
intro:
Van insurance turns on one question that car insurance never asks: what is the van actually for?

Social-only, carriage of own goods, and hire-and-reward are three different products at three very different prices, and declaring the wrong one is the most common reason a van claim gets refused. A tradesman who insures for social use because it was cheaper has effectively bought nothing.

Admiral's van proposition is built on the same foundations as its car cover — MultiCar, MultiCover, tiered comprehensive policies — but the use-class question sits in front of all of it, and it deserves more attention than the premium does.

sections.heading: Get the use class right or nothing else matters
sections.html:
Three classes, and the gap between them is the whole ballgame:

  • Social, domestic and pleasure — the van is personal transport. Cheapest, and useless to anyone working from it.
  • Carriage of own goods — you carry your own tools, stock or equipment for your own business. This is what most tradespeople need.
  • Hire and reward — you carry goods belonging to other people for payment. Couriers, deliveries, man-and-van work.

Insurers check use class when a claim is made, not when the premium is taken. A plumber insured social-only who crashes on the way to a job can find the claim declined and the policy voided — which then has to be declared on every future application.

The saving from under-declaring is typically modest. The consequence is total. If you use the van for work in any capacity, buy the class that reflects it.

sections.heading: Where MultiCar changes the calculation
sections.html:
Admiral's MultiCar scheme lets a van sit on the same policy as household cars, each keeping its own no-claims bonus.

This is genuinely useful for a sole trader with a work van and a family car, or a small operation running two vans and a car. The combined price is usually below the sum of separate policies, and there is one renewal date instead of three.

MultiCover adds home insurance to the bundle for a further discount — relevant if you are self-employed and working from home anyway.

The same caveat applies as with cars: vehicles generally need to be at the same address. A van kept at a yard or lock-up rather than your home may not qualify, and that is worth confirming before building a renewal strategy around it.

sections.heading: Tools are usually not covered, and that surprises people
sections.html:
Van insurance covers the van. It does not automatically cover what is inside it.

Tools cover is generally an add-on, and when you buy it there are three things to check rather than assume:

  • The limit. A working tradesman's van can hold £5,000 to £15,000 of equipment. Add-on limits are often far lower.
  • Overnight conditions. Many policies exclude theft from a van left on the street overnight, or require tools to be removed entirely between certain hours. This is the clause that defeats most tools claims.
  • Whether individual high-value items need listing. A £900 laser level may need naming specifically to be covered.

If tools are your livelihood, read this section of the policy wording before comparing premiums. A cheaper policy with a £1,000 tools limit and an overnight exclusion is not cheaper in any meaningful sense.

sections.heading: Two things to confirm before buying
sections.html:
Does the courtesy vehicle come as a van? A courtesy car is worthless to someone whose van is their working vehicle. Some policies provide a like-for-like van, some provide a small car, and some provide nothing on van policies at all. If your income depends on the vehicle, this is the most important line in the policy.

What are the cancellation terms? Admiral's fees run to £60–£160 to cancel and around £15 to amend. Vans change hands more often than cars — upgrading as a business grows, or downsizing when work is thin — so mid-term cancellation is a realistic scenario rather than a hypothetical one.

pros: MultiCar allows a van and household cars on one policy, each keeping its own no-claims bonus
MultiCover extends the discount to home insurance, useful for home-based sole traders
One renewal date instead of several across vehicles
Wide voluntary excess range for tuning the premium
Established insurer with 24/7 claims support
cons: Tools cover is generally an add-on rather than standard, with limits and overnight exclusions to check
Courtesy vehicle may not be a like-for-like van — confirm before buying
Cancellation fees of £60 to £160 matter more for vans, which change hands often
MultiCar generally requires vehicles at the same address, which rules out yard-kept vans
Use class must be declared accurately or a claim can be refused and the policy voided
verdict: Worth a quote if you have other vehicles to bundle — MultiCar is the strongest part of Admiral's proposition and a van sits in it naturally alongside a family car. Before comparing premiums, settle two things: declare the correct use class, because under-declaring voids the policy at the worst possible moment, and check whether tools cover and a like-for-like courtesy van are included or extra. For a working van those two clauses matter more than the price difference between insurers.

faqs.q: What use class do I need?
faqs.a: Social only if the van is purely personal transport. Carriage of own goods if you carry your own tools or stock for your business — this covers most tradespeople. Hire and reward if you carry other people's goods for payment. Declaring the wrong class can void the policy.

faqs.q: Are my tools covered?
faqs.a: Not usually as standard. Tools cover is generally an add-on. Check the limit, whether high-value items must be listed individually, and any overnight conditions — many policies exclude theft from a van left on the street overnight.

faqs.q: Will I get a courtesy van?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Some policies provide a like-for-like van, some a small car, some nothing at all on van cover. Confirm this specifically if the van is how you earn.

faqs.q: Can I put my van on a MultiCar policy?
faqs.a: Yes. Vans can sit alongside cars on one Admiral policy, each keeping its own no-claims bonus. Vehicles generally need to be at the same address, so a van kept at a separate yard may not qualify.

faqs.q: What does it cost to cancel?
faqs.a: Between £60 and £160 depending on circumstances, plus around £15 for amendments. Worth factoring in if you change vans regularly.

title: Quotezone.co.uk Car Insurance
meta_title: Quotezone Car Insurance: Compare 130+ UK Insurers
meta_description: Quotezone compares car insurance from over 130 UK providers, free to use and FCA regulated. How it works, what it costs, and what to check before you buy.
intro:
Quotezone has been comparing UK insurance since 2005, and built the country's first van insurance comparison the year after. Two decades on it runs around 5 million quotes a year for roughly 4 million users, across more than 60 insurance and financial products.

The comparison itself is free and always has been. It also holds ISO 27001 certification and is registered with the ICO as a data controller. For a service you hand your address, registration and claims history to, that is worth more than a badge on a homepage. The company is one of only 11 Ofgem-accredited energy comparison sites in the UK, which is a reasonable proxy for whether a comparison business is taken seriously.

sections.heading: Where car insurance pricing actually sits right now
sections.html:
Quotezone publishes its own index of average premiums, which is useful for judging whether a quote you have been given is normal:

  • Q1 2026: £579.52 average premium, down roughly 9% year on year
  • Q1 2025: £651.25

Premiums have fallen appreciably from that 2023 high. If your renewal quote has gone up while the market average has fallen 9%, that is worth challenging, and it is the single most useful thing on the site.

Treat these as market averages, not as your price. Age, postcode, vehicle group, mileage and claims history move an individual premium far more than the market trend does.

sections.heading: What the £535 figure actually measures
sections.html:
The advertised figure is £535.17. The small print underneath it is doing a great deal of work, and it is quoted here in full because the difference matters:

“51% of consumers could save £535.17 on their Car Insurance. The saving was calculated by comparing the cheapest price found with the average of the next four cheapest prices quoted by insurance providers on Seopa Ltd's insurance comparison website. This is based on representative cost savings from May 2026 data.”

Two things follow from that wording. The first is 51% — roughly half of people did not achieve it. The second is what the saving is measured against: the cheapest quote on the panel versus the average of the next four cheapest quotes on the same panel. It is not measured against your current premium, and it is not measured against the wider market.

So the number describes the spread between the best result and the near-misses on a single comparison run. That is a real thing to know — it says the top five results can differ by several hundred pounds, which is an argument for comparing at all. It is not a forecast of what you personally will save by switching.

sections.heading: How far the panel reaches
sections.html:
The car insurance pages state a panel of over 130 FCA-regulated UK providers. Seopa's own corporate site describes access to over 300 providers across all its products, and the site as a whole covers 60+ insurance and financial products. Those figures are not contradictory — one is a single product line, the other is the company total — but the larger number is the one that tends to get quoted, and it is not the car insurance panel.

More important is what the disclosure document says next: “providers make their own decisions as to whether they will use comparison services. Some do not. We do not claim to be whole of market.”

Direct Line has historically been the well-known example of an insurer that stays off comparison panels. A missing insurer is not evidence of a poor panel; it is a reason to treat any comparison result as the best price on that panel rather than the best price available anywhere.

sections.heading: Using it well, and what to do afterwards
sections.html:
The service is information-only by design, so the judgement is left to you. A few things follow from that:

  • Read the cover, not just the price. The cheapest result frequently carries a higher excess or a narrower definition of cover. Nothing on a comparison screen makes that comparison for you.
  • Check the monthly cost separately. Paying by instalments is credit, and the APR varies sharply between insurers on the same panel.
  • Run a second source. Because the panel is not whole of market, one direct quote from an insurer that stays off comparison sites is a sensible cross-check.
  • Expect contact. You are being introduced to providers, and the provider you select takes over the relationship from that point.

Complaints go to Seopa first. If it is not resolved within eight weeks you can take it to the Financial Ombudsman Service, and the Financial Services Compensation Scheme covers non-investment insurance mediation.

sections.heading: Buildings, contents, or the one policy that does both
sections.html:
The first thing the form asks is which of three products you want, and the answer changes the price more than any insurer choice you make afterwards.

Buildings insures the structure — walls, roof, floors, fitted kitchens and bathrooms, usually garages and boundary walls. A mortgage lender will insist on it. Contents insures what you would take with you if you moved. Combined puts both on one policy, and the arithmetic favours it strongly. The Association of British Insurers put the average combined premium at £379 in Q4 2025, against £312 for buildings alone and £122 for contents alone. Bought as two separate policies that is £434 — roughly £55 more for the same protection, plus a second excess and a second renewal date to remember.

Two figures on the form are yours to get right, and no comparison screen will check them for you.

  • Rebuild cost is not market value. It is what a builder would charge to clear the site and put the house back up. On older and rural properties it often exceeds what the house would sell for; on a city flat it is usually far less. Understate it and the insurer can apply average, scaling a claim down in proportion to the shortfall, so a half-insured house gets half of a £20,000 claim.
  • The contents sum insured should be what it would cost to replace everything, not what you paid. Walk the house room by room once and the figure is usually higher than the number people guess.

Single-item limits sit underneath the headline contents figure and typically bite somewhere between £1,500 and £2,500. Anything above that — a ring, a bike, a laptop, a watch — needs naming individually on the policy, and a comparison result will not tell you which insurers set that ceiling where.

An older Quotezone sample of 100,000 policies covering Q1 2023 to Q4 2024 priced detached homes at £308.66, semi-detached at £265.16, terraced at £259.38 and apartments at £160.07. That same dataset put the national average at £274.17 and recorded English premiums rising around 60% from the start of 2023, with London up 69%.

Those two datasets do not sit comfortably together, and the site does not reconcile them: a £274.17 national average from the older sample is higher than nine of the eleven regional figures published for Q2 2026. Treat the 2026 regional table as the current one and the property-type split as directional rather than exact.

Neither set matches the ABI's £379, and that is not a contradiction. Quotezone is reporting prices quoted on its own panel to people actively shopping around; the ABI is reporting premiums actually written across the whole market, including the renewals of people who never compared. The distance between those two numbers is roughly the value of shopping around at all.

sections.heading: Regulation, payment and who you argue with later
sections.html:
Seopa's FCA permissions cover insurance mediation and credit broking. The second one earns more attention than it usually gets. Paying for home insurance in twelve monthly instalments is a credit agreement, not a payment plan, and the APR attached to it varies sharply between insurers sitting side by side on the same results page. A policy that wins on annual premium can lose on the monthly figure, and the comparison screen ranks on the former.

The company is paid by the providers on its panel, as a flat fee, as commission, or as a mixture of the two. Nothing is added to what you pay, and Seopa says so in its own disclosure document rather than leaving you to work it out. It is also registered with the Information Commissioner's Office as a data controller under Z8733752, which matters for a service you hand your full address, security arrangements and claims history to.

What you do not get is advice. Seopa states plainly that it makes no recommendation and does not tell you which policy to take, so every judgement about excess levels, accidental damage, home emergency and legal expenses cover is left with you. Nothing on the results screen shows a Defaqto star rating or a Fairer Finance score for the insurers listed, and both are worth ten minutes of separate checking before you commit — a five-star rated policy and a one-star policy can appear a pound apart.

The complaint routes split in two, and knowing which is which saves time:

  • About the comparison service — the quote, the data, the website — goes to Seopa, which aims to respond by the next working day after receiving it. If it is still unresolved after eight weeks, or once you have a final response, the Financial Ombudsman Service will take it. You have six months from that final response letter to refer it.
  • About the policy or a claim goes to the insurer, not to Seopa. Seopa introduced you; it is not a party to your cover.

The Financial Services Compensation Scheme covers non-investment insurance mediation at 90% of the claim with no upper limit.

sections.heading: Flood, subsidence and the houses a standard form cannot price
sections.html:
UK insurers paid a record £6.1 billion in property claims during 2025, of which £1.2 billion was weather-related — a 14% rise worth £142 million on the year before. The average property claim climbed 15%, up almost £800 to around £6,000. Those numbers are why the questions about your postcode's flood history and any past cracking are the ones insurers price hardest.

The detail underneath is sharper still. Domestic flood claims rose 38% to £312 million and the average flood payout jumped 60% to £30,000. Storm damage to homes reached £244 million, up 32%, with the average storm claim at £2,450 — £750 more than in 2024. Subsidence payouts hit £307 million, up 10%.

If your home has flooded, Flood Re is the mechanism that keeps it insurable, and it works behind the scenes: your insurer cedes the flood element of the risk to the scheme. Eligibility is specific rather than automatic. The property must be in council tax bands A to H, built before 1 January 2009, used privately and residentially, insured in an individual's name, and be a single unit or part of a building of no more than three. Blocks of more than three flats, housing association buildings and commercially let property fall outside it. The scheme is funded to run until 2039, after which flood premiums are expected to move to risk-reflective pricing.

Empty property is the other place the form runs out of road. Most home policies stop covering a house after 30 to 60 consecutive days without anyone living in it, and the exact figure differs by insurer — a probate sale, a renovation or a long gap between tenants can quietly void cover without anything visibly changing. Quotezone routes that to a separate unoccupied product, where the panel is a handful of specialist brokers rather than the 40-plus insurers quoting mainstream risks. The same applies to listed buildings and thatch.

sections.heading: The £257.05 figure, unpicked
sections.html:
The headline on the home insurance page is a saving of £257.05, and the footnote beneath it is doing most of the work. Quoted in full: "51% of consumers could save £257.05 on their Home Building & Contents Insurance. The saving was calculated by comparing the cheapest price found with the average of the next fourteen cheapest prices quoted by insurance providers on Seopa Ltd's insurance comparison website. This is based on representative cost savings from April 2026."

Three things follow. The first is 51% — just over half of people reached it, and the other half did not. The second is what the saving is measured against: not your existing premium, and not the wider market, but the average of the fourteen results sitting immediately behind the winner on the same panel. The third is the size of that comparison basket. Widening it from a handful of runners-up to fourteen pulls the average being compared against upwards, because the fourteenth cheapest quote is a long way behind the first. The figure is a fair description of how far apart prices on one panel can be. It is not a forecast of what you will save by switching.

Two structural limits belong here too. The home panel is stated at 40+ providers, against the 130+ Quotezone advertises for car insurance — a materially narrower field, and Seopa does not claim to be whole of market, since some insurers decline to appear on comparison services at all. And since 1 January 2022, FCA rules have required firms to quote a renewing home insurance customer no more than they would quote a new customer through the same channel, which has compressed the loyalty penalty that made switching so dramatically profitable a few years ago. Comparing still pays. It pays less than a headline built on 2019 behaviour would suggest.

One last habit worth keeping: the cheapest line on the results page frequently gets there through a higher excess, a lower single-item limit or accidental damage stripped out. Open two or three policy documents before you choose, because the ranking is by price and nothing on the screen ranks by cover.

sections.heading: Ten routes behind one questionnaire
sections.html:
Splitting the form by tenancy type is the sensible part of this product, because a two-bed flat let to a working couple and a six-bed house let room by room are priced by different underwriters on different assumptions. Send the second one down the standard buildings route and the quote you get back is worthless.

The routes that matter most:

  • HMO — any property let to several unrelated tenants sharing kitchen or bathroom. Fire risk, licensing and tenant turnover all price separately.
  • Blocks of flats — freeholder cover for the structure and communal parts, which a single-dwelling policy does not contemplate.
  • Student and DSS lets — declared honestly, these narrow the panel rather than voiding it. Declared dishonestly, they hand the insurer a reason to walk away from a claim.
  • Unoccupied — between tenancies, during refurbishment, or through a probate sale.
  • Multi-property — one schedule, one renewal date, for portfolios that would otherwise mean five separate arguments every spring.

The scale question sits behind all of it. There are roughly 2.8 million landlords in the UK, and 86% of them hold fewer than five properties, so the typical user of this form is somebody letting one or two houses alongside a day job rather than a professional portfolio operator. That same research found around 400,000 landlords carrying no specialist cover at all — in most cases an ordinary residential policy quietly doing a job it was never written for.

sections.heading: The law moved under this product on 1 May 2026
sections.html:
Anything written about landlord insurance before this year is now describing a different legal position, and the products on the panel have had to move with it.

The Renters' Rights Act 2025 took Royal Assent on 27 October 2025 and its main provisions bit on 1 May 2026. Assured shorthold tenancies became assured periodic tenancies overnight, no new fixed terms can be granted, and Section 21 no-fault possession is gone. Old Section 21 notices became time-barred where a claim form had not been requested by 31 July 2026, and landlords had until 31 May 2026 to give every tenant the government information sheet, with a penalty of up to £7,000 for those who did not.

Possession now runs entirely through Section 8 grounds, and the timings are what your insurance has to survive:

  • Ground 8, rent arrears — two months' arrears, 4 weeks notice, and the arrears must still stand at two months on the day of the hearing. A tenant who pays down a few hundred pounds the week before court can collapse the case.
  • Grounds 1 and 1A, moving in or selling — 3 months notice, and neither can be served during the first 12 months of a tenancy.
  • Ground 14, serious anti-social behaviour — two weeks, or proceedings from the day after service in the worst cases.

Two more dates are coming: the private rented sector database begins rolling out regionally from late 2026, a landlord ombudsman becomes compulsory in 2028, and the Decent Homes Standard reaches private lettings by 2035.

The practical consequence for anyone using this comparison is that rent guarantee and legal expenses cover have stopped being optional nice-to-haves. When the quickest lawful route to an empty house was two months and a Section 21 notice, a landlord could self-insure a void. A contested Section 8 claim through a court list is a different length of exposure.

sections.html:
This is the add-on the comparison will offer you and the one most worth reading properly. Alan Boswell's product, as a representative example of what the panel quotes, prices at £195 for 12 months bought alongside a landlord policy or £250 standalone, and pays:

  • Up to £2,500 of rent a month
  • Up to 15 months of rental cover, plus 3 months after eviction at 75% of the monthly rent
  • Legal expenses up to £100,000

The eligibility rules are where these policies are won and lost, and they apply to the tenant you already have as much as the next one. Referencing typically requires two forms of identification, one photographic; tenants clear of CCJs, IVAs and bankruptcy for at least three years; and affordability evidenced at 2.5 times the monthly rent, rising to 3 times for the self-employed.

Then the paperwork on your side. A written tenancy agreement has to be in place, and the gas safety certificate, the EPC and the deposit prescribed information all have to have reached the tenant. Miss any of those and you have bought a policy that cannot pay, because you cannot lawfully take possession.

The claims clock is tighter than it looks. Cover engages after the second missed payment, and while you have 90 days to notify a claim, notification between day 61 and day 90 costs you a month's rent off the settlement. A landlord who spends eight weeks trying to sort things out amicably with a tenant they like has already given up several hundred pounds.

sections.heading: Liability, empty weeks and the price of the wrong property type
sections.html:
Property owners' liability is the cover a landlord is least likely to think about and most likely to need in a serious way. It answers for injury caused by the condition of the building — a loose slate, a rotten stair tread, failed guttering over a pavement — and the Defective Premises Act makes that a duty rather than a courtesy. £2 million is the ordinary benchmark for a residential letting, with £5 million and above normal on commercial premises. Bought on its own it is generally a £50 to £200 line, which is a small sum against a claim that would otherwise land on you personally.

Empty weeks are the other place a policy quietly stops working. Cover on a standard landlord contract usually falls away somewhere between the 30th and 60th consecutive day of an unoccupied house, and Quotezone's own guidance makes the point that the counting begins the day the tenant hands the keys back, not the day the builders arrive. A void between tenancies plus a fortnight of redecoration will cross the line at a good many insurers, and telling them beforehand costs nothing while telling them afterwards is a declined claim.

The type of property you let moves the premium more than most landlords expect. On the 2026 market analysis, terraced houses accounted for 49% of all landlord quotes at a median of £269.47, semi-detached houses 19.91% of quotes at around £280, while purpose-built blocks of flats came in at £822.84 — roughly three times the terraced figure. If you are moving from a house into a flat conversion, budget for that gap rather than assuming your renewal will follow you across.

For context on what these policies are paying out against, insurers settled £6.1 billion of UK property claims across 2025, and the average claim value rose by 15% to sit near £6,000. Subsidence alone accounted for £307 million.

sections.heading: What the panel is actually made of
sections.html:
Look carefully at the names quoting on the landlord form and a pattern shows up that is not there on the car insurance side. Coversure, Gallagher, Howden, Swinton, Jensten, Specialist Risk Group, Konsileo, Aldium, Gauntlet, Cover4LetProperty: these are brokers and schemes, not insurers writing risk on their own paper. That is normal for landlord business, which is a broker market, and it is how you get access to underwriters who will look at an HMO or a listed cottage at all.

It does have a cost, though, and it is one the comparison screen does not show you. A broker-arranged policy can carry its own arrangement fee, amendment fee and cancellation fee sitting on top of the insurer's premium, and those are disclosed in the broker's terms rather than in the quote you are ranking on. Two results a few pounds apart on screen can be £50 apart once the paperwork arrives. Ask the fee question before you buy, on any quote you are seriously considering.

Three further limits are worth naming plainly. Seopa states in its own disclosure document that it does not claim to be whole of market and that "you will not receive advice or a recommendation from us", so every judgement about liability limits, excesses and whether malicious damage by tenants is in or out is left with you. No Defaqto star rating or Fairer Finance score appears anywhere on the results, and on landlord products the difference between a five-star and a one-star policy is mostly in the clauses you only read after something has gone wrong. And unlike the car and home pages, which advertise savings of £535.17 and £257.05 respectively, there is no published saving figure for landlord cover at all, so you have no benchmark from the site itself for what comparing is worth here.

One last mechanical point: paying monthly is a credit agreement rather than a payment plan, and the APR varies between providers sitting next to each other on the same results page. The ranking you are shown is by annual premium, so the cheapest line on screen is not reliably the cheapest twelve monthly payments.

Separate routes for HMO, blocks of flats, student, DSS, multi-property and unoccupied risks rather than one generic form
FCA authorised under firm reference 313860, covering insurance mediation and credit broking
Broker-heavy panel is how you reach underwriters willing to look at non-standard lettings
Rent guarantee and legal expenses quoted alongside buildings cover, which matters more since Section 21 was abolished
Straightforward disclosure of how the business earns and what it does not do
Operating since 2005 under the same ownership, and ICO registered as a data controller
cons: The panel is largely brokers and schemes rather than insurers, so arrangement, amendment and cancellation fees can sit on top of the premium without appearing in the comparison
No advertised saving figure for landlord cover, unlike the £535.17 and £257.05 headlines on the car and home pages, so the site offers no benchmark for what comparing is worth
Not whole of market, and no advice or recommendation is given on liability limits, excesses or exclusions
No Defaqto or Fairer Finance rating appears on any result, despite landlord policies varying widely on clauses
The 4.71/5 score from 3,435 reviews is Quotezone's own on-site figure rather than an independently audited one
Specialist routes — unoccupied, listed, blocks of flats — reach a much smaller set of providers than the headline 35+
Monthly payment is credit with an APR that varies by provider, and results are ranked on annual premium instead

verdict: A sensible first stop for a landlord with one or two ordinary lettings who wants to know whether a renewal is out of line, and a genuinely useful one for anybody whose property does not fit a standard form — the separate HMO, block of flats, student, DSS and unoccupied routes reach underwriters a mainstream home insurance comparison never will. Judge the results against the £284.75 median rather than against last year's premium, and ask every broker you shortlist what its arrangement and cancellation fees are, because those sit outside the price you are ranking on. Since possession now runs through Section 8 alone, price rent guarantee and legal expenses properly rather than treating them as extras, and check your gas safety certificate, EPC and deposit paperwork are all served before you buy a policy whose payout depends on them.

faqs.q: How many landlord insurers does Quotezone compare?
faqs.a: The landlord pages state 35 or more providers. Most are brokers and schemes rather than insurers writing on their own paper, and Seopa does not claim to cover the whole market — treat any result as the best price on that panel rather than the best available anywhere.

faqs.q: Is landlord insurance a legal requirement?
faqs.a: No, but buy-to-let lenders routinely make buildings cover a condition of the mortgage, and property owners' liability protects you against injury claims arising from the state of the building. Around 2.8 million UK landlords are letting property, and roughly 400,000 of them hold no specialist cover.

faqs.q: What happens to my cover between tenancies?
faqs.a: Most standard landlord policies stop responding once a property has stood empty for somewhere between 30 and 60 consecutive days, and the count begins the day the tenant leaves rather than the day work starts. Tell your insurer before the gap opens, or use the separate unoccupied route.

faqs.q: Is rent guarantee insurance worth buying now Section 21 has gone?
faqs.a: It carries more weight than it used to. Since 1 May 2026 possession runs entirely through Section 8, where a rent arrears claim needs two months of arrears still standing at the hearing after 4 weeks' notice. Representative pricing runs from around £195 for 12 months, covering up to £2,500 of monthly rent and legal costs to £100,000, but the tenant has to meet the referencing standard and your own paperwork has to be in order.

faqs.q: Does it cost anything to use, and who do I complain to?
faqs.a: Nothing — the providers pay Seopa a fee, a commission or both, and the premium quoted is the provider's own. Anything about the comparison itself goes to Seopa and then, after eight weeks or a final response, to the Financial Ombudsman Service. Anything about the policy or a claim goes to the insurer or broker instead.

intro:
Bike insurance is a stubbornly manual market. Plenty of the firms that price a 125cc commuter, a restored Bonneville and a 200bhp adventure bike sensibly are small brokers with schemes rather than household-name insurers, and finding them one at a time is an evening's work. Quotezone puts up to 25 motorbike providers behind a single questionnaire and hands back their prices in a few minutes, at no charge to the rider — the introduction is paid for at the provider end.

The business behind the brand is Seopa Limited, incorporated in Belfast on 25 April 2003 and running the Quotezone site since 2005. On its own bike pages it reports a satisfaction score of 4.83 out of 5 and says 97% of reviewers would recommend it.

Carry one number in with you. Quotezone's own headline is that 51% of riders quoted through the service in May 2026 were shown a price under £256.34. That is a quote threshold rather than an average paid, but it gives you a rough sense of where an ordinary bike on an ordinary postcode ought to land, which is what turns a screen of prices into something you can judge.

sections.heading: One form, three cover levels and a lot of bike shapes
sections.html:
The questionnaire runs the three statutory tiers. Third party only is the legal floor and pays for injury and damage you cause to other people. Third party, fire and theft adds the two losses that account for most bikes that never come back. Comprehensive brings in damage to your own machine, and on a bike it is often no dearer than the middle tier, because insurers read it as a signal about the rider rather than the risk.

What matters more on two wheels is the extras list, and the panel quotes on most of it: pillion cover, helmet and leathers, personal effects, legal expenses, European use, protected no-claims discount and breakdown. Helmet and leathers is the one riders underestimate — a lid and a set of textiles can run past £1,000, and a comprehensive policy will not automatically pay for either.

The machine list stretches well past road bikes to mopeds, scooters, quads, 50cc and 125cc learner bikes and classics. One entry on that list needs care: Quotezone also names electric scooters, and privately owned e-scooters remain illegal to use on public land anywhere in Great Britain. Only rental scooters in designated trial areas are permitted, they are limited to 15.5mph, and the operator supplies the third-party cover, so there is nothing for a rider to buy.

sections.heading: Who Seopa answers to, and who pays it
sections.html:
Seopa holds FCA permission as a non-investment insurance intermediary and a credit broker, which is the correct shape of authorisation for a firm that introduces you to insurers and to the finance arrangement behind monthly payments. Its insurance mediation falls within the Financial Services Compensation Scheme: 90% of a claim with no upper limit for ordinary insurance mediation, and 100% with no upper limit for compulsory classes, which is the bracket bike insurance sits in.

The company is candid about payment. Its initial disclosure document states that providers pay "a flat fee, a commission or a combination of the two", and the how-we-make-money page ties that payment to a completed sale rather than a click. The same document is equally blunt about the limits of the service: "You will not receive advice or a recommendation from us", and the panel "do not claim to be whole of market".

If something goes wrong with the introduction itself, complaints go to Seopa Customer Relations in Belfast, and to the Financial Ombudsman Service at Exchange Tower, Harbour Exchange Square, London E14 9SR, or 0800 023 4567, once eight weeks have passed. That route is worth knowing about. In 2024/25 the ombudsman took 14,082 complaints about car and motorcycle insurance and upheld 42% of them, against 38% across insurance generally and 34% across every financial product it handles.

sections.heading: What a bike quote is really reacting to
sections.html:
Two forces are pulling in opposite directions on price. Riding is getting more popular: L-category registrations in May 2026 were up 14.9% on the same month a year earlier, with the year to date up 15.8%, adventure bikes up 29.1% in the month and road sport up 22.8%. More new machines on the road usually means more theft-attractive stock and more claims.

Against that, the underlying motor market has cooled. The Association of British Insurers put the average motor premium at £560 in the first quarter of 2026, down 3.6% on a year earlier, though repair costs have not followed — insurers paid out £2.9bn in the quarter, £1.9bn of it on repairs, with the average accidental damage claim up 8% to £3,699.

Then there is the risk the underwriter is actually pricing. Department for Transport figures record 315 motorcyclists killed and 5,481 seriously injured in a single year, a rate of 111 deaths per billion vehicle miles across 2.85bn miles ridden. That rate, not your postcode, is why a bike premium behaves so differently from a car one — and it is also why the trend is better than riders expect, with fatalities down 46% since 2004 while traffic fell only a tenth.

sections.heading: The rules that turn a cheap quote into an expensive week
sections.html:
Insurance on a bike used on the road is compulsory, and the penalties are not proportionate to the saving. A police stop without cover brings a £300 fixed penalty and 6 points, the court can add an unlimited fine and a disqualification, and the machine can be seized and in some cases destroyed.

The licence rules catch people out just as often, because the quote form asks about entitlement and the answer changes the price. Category AM starts at 16 and covers mopeds restricted to 45km/h. A1 starts at 17 and allows up to 125cc and 11kW. A2 starts at 19 and caps power at 35kW. Unrestricted category A is 24 by direct access, or 21 by progressive access from A2.

Compulsory basic training lasts 2 years, and letting it lapse without passing the full test carries a fine of up to £1,000 and up to 6 penalty points. Buy a year's policy on a CBT with four months left on it and you are paying for cover you cannot legally use for two thirds of the term.

sections.heading: Where the service stops short
sections.html:
The panel is the first limit. Up to 25 providers is a decent spread for a bike, but Seopa says plainly that it is not whole of market, and the specialist end of motorcycling — classic valuations, multi-bike policies, track day extensions, heavily modified machines — is exactly where a single missing broker costs you real money. Anyone with an unusual bike should ring two direct-only names as well.

The second is contact. Quotezone's privacy policy confirms that the three cheapest online providers may get in touch, and that the telephone service allows up to 5 providers to call, with email, SMS and WhatsApp on top where consent has been given. Providers may also run a soft credit search, which shows on your file without affecting your rating. None of that is hidden, but it is more contact than a rider comparing prices out of curiosity expects.

The third is the gap between a quote and a price. Seopa's own terms say the display of a quote "is not a representation from us that insurance will be available to you at the price shown", and the £256.34 figure is the level half of May's quotes fell below rather than a typical amount paid. Results are ordered on price, so excess levels, modification rules and claims handling do not surface until you click through — and Defaqto rates the policies on that panel, not the comparison service carrying them. The satisfaction score is thin evidence too: 4.83 out of 5 is a strong number, but it rests on 141 reviews from a service running millions of quotes a year. One loose end worth flagging: the initial disclosure PDF still shows an Adelaide Street address while Companies House and the site's legal page both give Amelia Street, so the document appears to be overdue an update.

pros: Up to 25 bike providers from one form, several of them scheme brokers you would not find individually
Free to use, with providers paying a flat fee or commission only when a policy is bought
FCA authorised as an intermediary under reference 313860, with FSCS protection at 100% for compulsory motor cover
Quotes mopeds, quads, 50cc and 125cc learner bikes and classics, not only mainstream road machines
Open about its own limits: no advice given, and no claim to cover the whole market
Belfast operation trading since 2003, with a published complaints route through to the Financial Ombudsman Service
cons: Not whole of market by its own admission, and specialist classic, multi-bike and modified risks are the likeliest to be missed
Your details reach the three cheapest providers, and the phone route allows up to 5 firms to call you
A displayed quote is explicitly not a guarantee of that price, and the £256.34 headline is a quote threshold rather than an average premium
Results rank on price alone, so excess, modification rules and claims handling stay invisible until you click through
The 4.83 out of 5 satisfaction figure rests on just 141 reviews against millions of quotes
The initial disclosure document carries an out-of-date registered address, which is a small but avoidable inconsistency in a regulated document
verdict: For an ordinary bike on an ordinary licence, Quotezone does the job it claims to: one form, up to 25 prices, nothing to pay, and a regulated firm with more than twenty years of trading behind it. Treat £256.34 as a sanity check rather than a target, expect three providers to contact you, and read the excess before the premium. Riders with a classic, a modified machine or a garage full of bikes should use it as a first sweep and then phone the specialists it does not carry.

faqs.q: Does Quotezone insure my motorbike itself?
faqs.a: No. Seopa Limited is an intermediary, not an insurer. It collects your details once, passes them to a panel of up to 25 providers and shows you what they quote. The policy, the excess, the claims line and the certificate all come from whichever provider you buy from.

faqs.q: Is the £256.34 figure what I should expect to pay?
faqs.a: Not exactly. It is the level that 51% of motorbike quotes issued through the service in May 2026 came in below — a quote threshold, not an average premium, and not a promise. Seopa's terms state that a quote on screen is not a representation that cover will be available at that price once the insurer has your full details.

faqs.a: Some will. The privacy policy allows the three cheapest online providers to make contact, and the telephone comparison route allows up to 5 providers to call, with email, SMS and WhatsApp used where you have given consent. Preferences can be changed through the site's opt-out centre, though quote confirmations still come through.

faqs.q: What happens if the comparison service itself lets me down?
faqs.a: Complain to Seopa Customer Relations in Belfast first. It upheld 42% of the 14,082 car and motorcycle insurance complaints it took in 2024/25.

faqs.q: Does comparing on price alone cost me anything on a bike?
faqs.a: It can. Bike policies differ sharply on helmet and leathers limits, pillion cover, modification declarations and whether a European trip is included. Two quotes twenty pounds apart can carry excesses hundreds of pounds apart, so the cheapest line on the results page is a starting point for reading the wording rather than a decision.

intro:
A tradesman rarely buys one policy. Quotezone puts that shape behind a single questionnaire, sends it out to the commercial brokers and insurers on its panel, and returns their prices free to the person filling it in.

Panel width counts for more on trade cover than it does on a car policy, because underwriting appetite splits hard by occupation: the insurer that wants a painter and decorator often will not look at a scaffolder at any price. Quotezone quotes plasterers, plumbers, electricians, carpenters, scaffolders, painters and general contractors, and describes public liability limits running “from £1 million up to £5 million, although some policies will cover you up to as much as £10 million”.

sections.heading: Four covers behind one questionnaire
sections.html:
The tradesman form gathers trade, turnover, staff numbers and work type once, then splits the answers across products that are legally and practically distinct. Public liability answers for injury to a member of the public or damage to their property caused by your work — the drilled pipe, the dropped scaffold board, the customer who trips over a cable run. Employers' liability answers for injury to the people who work for you. They are different obligations with different triggers, and buying one does nothing for the other.

Alongside those, the tradesman pages quote tools and equipment cover, legal expenses, and business buildings and contents for anyone with a yard, workshop or lock-up. A limit of £1 million is the entry point across most of the panel, £2 million and £5 million the common steps above it, and £10 million available on schemes built for larger sites. The number is worth checking against your paperwork before you shop: main contractors, housing associations and local authority frameworks routinely set the limit they will accept, and a quote £40 cheaper at £1m is worthless if the job needs £5m.

What sits behind each result varies. Some marks on the page are insurers writing their own risk; others, Gallagher and Coversure among them, are brokers who will place the risk with an insurer of their choosing. That mix is normal in commercial lines and generally works in a tradesman's favour, because a broker can put an awkward occupation in front of an underwriter who would never appear on a price comparison table. It also means the return time varies: an instant online price and a broker who rings back are both possible outcomes of the same form.

sections.heading: The day a first employee makes cover compulsory
sections.html:
Employers' liability is where the law stops advising and starts requiring. Under the Employers' Liability (Compulsory Insurance) Act 1969, the Health and Safety Executive's guidance is blunt about the level: “You must be insured for at least £5 million”, though in practice most insurers issue £10 million as standard. Trade without it and you can be fined up to £2,500 for each day you are uninsured. Fail to display the certificate or refuse it to an HSE inspector and that is a further £1,000.

Two details catch out small firms. Since 1 October 2008 there has been no legal duty to keep expired certificates, but the HSE still advises holding them, because industrial disease claims surface decades after exposure and the certificate is what identifies which insurer answers for the year in question. And the exemptions are narrower than the trade talk suggests: a family business where every employee is a close relative is outside the Act, as is a limited company whose only employee owns 50% or more of the share capital, but take on one apprentice from outside the family and the duty starts that morning.

The risk is not theoretical in the building trades. In its latest annual figures the HSE records 126 workers killed in work-related accidents, 59,219 employee injuries reported under RIDDOR, 680,000 people reporting an injury at work in the Labour Force Survey, and 40.1 million working days lost to injury and work-related illness. It puts the annual cost of injury and ill health from current working conditions at £22.9 billion for 2023/24. Construction contributes disproportionately to all of it.

sections.heading: Reading a tools add-on before you need to claim on it
sections.html:
Tools cover is the cheapest line on a tradesman quote and the one most likely to disappoint, because the price is set by conditions the comparison stage never shows you. Take the published terms of one specialist tradesman insurer, Rhino Trade Insurance, as a worked example of the shape: cover from £4.74 a month, or £56.86 for the year, with limits from £500 up to £7,500 and an excess of £100 on each and every claim. Whether that particular scheme appears on the Quotezone panel needs confirming, but the structure is the market's.

The conditions are where the money goes. Overnight cover in a vehicle runs between 10pm and 6am and depends on where the van is parked — a locked garage, your own driveway, or a street in clear view of where you are sleeping. Theft with no sign of forced entry is out. Tools on display in an unlocked vehicle are out. Kit stored anywhere other than the vehicle can be out entirely. Settlement is reduced by 10% depreciation for every year of a tool's age up to a ceiling of 50%, so a five-year-old SDS drill pays out at half its replacement price, and receipts matter because proof of purchase is a condition rather than a courtesy.

One structural point that changes how you shop: on several schemes tools cover is only sold to customers who hold the same insurer's public liability policy. Buying the cheapest liability from one result and the cheapest tools cover from another is not always an option, which makes the combined price the number to compare rather than the headline one.

sections.heading: Belfast, the regulator, and the protections a business does and does not get
sections.html:
Seopa Ltd is authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority under reference 313860, registered in Northern Ireland as NI46322, and its terms describe its permitted business as “insurance mediation as well as having permission for credit brokerage”, acting as a “non-investment insurance intermediary” and not as a lender. Nothing you buy is a contract with Seopa. The policy, and the promise to pay a claim, belongs to the insurer named on the certificate.

Payment is disclosed plainly: the company “may receive a commission and/or other remuneration from providers, insurers, intermediaries, or other third parties” when you click through, enquire or buy, and its terms invite you to ask for details of what it earns on your particular transaction. Few buyers ever do, and on commercial risks placed through a broker the remuneration can be a meaningful slice of the premium. Whatever is quoted, the standard Insurance Premium Tax rate of 12% is already inside the figure you see.

The part that actually differs for a trade buyer is what happens when something goes wrong. Complaints about the introduction go to Seopa in Belfast, which works to eight weeks before the Financial Ombudsman Service can take over, and a referral must reach the Ombudsman within six months of the final response letter. But a business is only eligible if it is small enough: annual turnover under £6.5 million, fewer than 50 employees or a balance sheet under £5 million, and the complaint must concern an act or omission on or after 1 April 2019. Most sole traders and small firms clear that comfortably. Ombudsman data also shows commercial cases are decided against the firm more often than average: 39% of commercial property complaints and 44% of commercial vehicle complaints were upheld in 2025/26, against 30% across all financial products.

sections.heading: Where the comparison hands the work back to you
sections.html:
No price appears anywhere on the tradesman pages before you complete the form. The site sets out cover levels and legal duties well, then answers the cost question by saying it depends on the trade and the risk profile, which is true and unhelpful in equal measure. There is no indicative premium by trade, no typical excess, and no published list of who is actually on the panel — the 30+ logos are a display, not a roster, and the site quotes panel sizes inconsistently elsewhere.

Professional indemnity is the notable absence from the tradesman line-up. Any trade that specifies, designs or certifies as well as installs — a plumber sizing a heating system, an electrician signing off an installation certificate — carries a professional risk that public liability does not touch. Quotezone sells professional indemnity elsewhere on the site, but it is not part of the tradesman journey, so a buyer who does not already know the distinction will not be prompted to make it.

Support is email only. The company states it does not currently provide a telephone service and aims to reply within two working days, with office hours of 9am to 5pm Monday to Friday. For a trade waiting on a certificate before starting on site, two days is a long time, and the company is clear that any question about the policy itself belongs to the insurer rather than to Quotezone. Your details may also be passed to the providers you are matched with, so expect broker follow-up by phone and email once the form is submitted.
